A sinew is a tendon — the tough, cord-like tissue inside your body that connects muscle to bone. When you say someone or something is sinewy, you are saying they have the qualities of that tissue: lean, tough, strong, and visibly muscular — without being soft, puffy, or bulky.

It is the kind of strength that looks worked for and lived in, not inflated.

When used to describe a person or animal, sinewy means:

  • The muscles are lean and defined, not hidden under fat or puffed up like a balloon.
  • The body looks tight and ropey — you can almost see the muscles and tendons working under the skin, like cables pulling under a surface.
  • It suggests toughness and endurance, not just size.

Think of a long-distance runner, a rock climber, a seasoned blacksmith, or a wild horse. They are not enormous or bulky — but every part of them is hard, useful muscle. There is no excess. That is sinewy.

Compare this to a bodybuilder, whose muscles are large and rounded. A bodybuilder is muscular or brawny. A marathon runner, however, is sinewy — lean, striated, tough as rope.

Examples in sentences:

  • His arms were sinewy from years of pulling nets out of the sea.
  • The old farmer was small but sinewy, and he worked harder than men half his age.
  • The greyhound's sinewy body was built for nothing but pure speed.

This contrast is very important for remembering the word:

Instead of...Sinewy means...
Soft, doughy, or flabbyLean and hard
Puffy or inflated (like a bodybuilder)Tight and ropey, like cable
Weak or thinStrong and capable
Hidden or invisible muscleClearly defined, visible muscle

Sinewy is not soft or flabby. It is not the inflated, rounded look of someone purely focused on size. And it is not just "thin" or "skinny" — a skinny person may have no muscle at all. A sinewy person is genuinely, functionally strong — just without the bulk.

This is where the word becomes especially interesting and powerful.

When "sinewy" is applied to writing, speech, or arguments, it carries the same idea over from the body: strong, lean, and without unnecessary flab. Sinewy writing is:

  • Direct and powerful — it gets to the point without wasting words.
  • Tight and forceful — every sentence does real work, like a muscle doing its job.
  • Hard to dismiss or ignore — it has real strength behind it.

Just as a sinewy body has no excess fat, sinewy prose has no excess words.

Ernest Hemingway's writing is a classic example people describe as sinewy — short, stripped-back sentences that hit hard precisely because they carry no fluff. A sinewy argument is one that is logical, tight, and difficult to argue against.

Examples in sentences:

  • The lawyer made a sinewy case — every point was precise, and there was nothing loose to pick apart.
  • Her writing style was sinewy: short sentences, strong verbs, no decoration.
  • The speech was not poetic or flowery, but it was sinewy and convincing.
A Less Common Use (Food and Meat)

When describing meat or food, sinewy simply means tough and stringy — containing actual sinew (tendons). This is almost always a negative quality in this context.

  • The steak was overcooked and sinewy — almost impossible to chew.

This usage is the most literal of all: the meat actually contains tough, fibrous tendons.
One Sentence to Capture It All

Sinewy means lean and visibly tough-strong — whether describing a person's muscles, an animal's body, or the way a piece of writing or an argument is built: no excess, no softness, just hard, functional, cord-like strength.
Think of the word sinew (a tough tendon) sitting right inside sinewy. Whenever you see the word, picture a tendon — tough, lean, ropey, built for pulling hard. That image is the meaning.
